\chapter{Chapter08 — Recursive Majority Decision Trees}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from FABL.Chapter08.RecursiveMajorityDecisionTrees
\section{Overview}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{FABL.Chapter08.RecursiveMajorityDecisionTrees}.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Three-input majority with one fixed input]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeFixedOneInput}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p021-b001}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeFixedOneInput}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube}
For an index $i\in\{0,1,2\}$ and signs $a,s\in\{-1,1\}$, define a three-coordinate sign
vector whose value at coordinate $i$ is $a$ and whose values at the other two
coordinates are both $s$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Three-coordinate majority with one fixed input]
\lean{FABL.majority_majorityThreeFixedOneInput}
\label{FABL.majority_majorityThreeFixedOneInput}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreeFixedOneInput, FABL.signValue, FABL.thresholdSign}
\difficulty{4}
Let $i$ be one of the three coordinate positions, and let $a,s\in\{-1,1\}$. The majority
of the three-coordinate vector whose $i$th entry is $a$ and whose other entries are both
$s$ equals $s$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Three-coordinate input with two fixed values]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeFixedTwoInput}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeFixedTwoInput}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube}
For indices $i,j\in\{0,1,2\}$ and signs $a,b,s\in\{-1,1\}$, form the three-coordinate
sign vector that is constantly $s$, then set coordinate $i$ to $a$ and coordinate $j$ to
$b$. If $i=j$, the value at that coordinate is $b$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Three-coordinate majority with two fixed inputs]
\lean{FABL.majority_majorityThreeFixedTwoInput}
\label{FABL.majority_majorityThreeFixedTwoInput}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreeFixedTwoInput, FABL.signValue, FABL.thresholdSign}
\difficulty{4}
Let $i,j$ be distinct positions among three coordinates, and let $a,b,s$ be signs with
$a\ne b$. The majority of the vector whose $i$th entry is $a$, whose $j$th entry is $b$,
and whose remaining entry is $s$ equals $s$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Initial query structure for majority trees]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.exists_majorityThree_querySkeleton}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.exists_majorityThree_querySkeleton}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval, FABL.Sign, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreeFixedOneInput, FABL.majorityThreeFixedTwoInput, FABL.majority_majorityThreeFixedOneInput, FABL.majority_majorityThreeFixedTwoInput, FABL.signValue, FABL.thresholdSign}
\difficulty{6}
Let $T$ be a decision tree on three coordinates with sign-valued inputs and outputs that
computes majority, with ties assigned the positive sign. Its root must query some
coordinate $i$. For each sign $a$, the corresponding child must query some coordinate
$j\ne i$; for each sign $b\ne a$, the resulting child must query some coordinate $k$
distinct from both $i$ and $j$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Query lower bound for three-bit majority]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.exists_majorityThree_first_second}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.exists_majorityThree_first_second}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.exists_majorityThree_querySkeleton, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace, FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.majority}
\difficulty{4}
Let $T$ be a decision tree on three coordinates with sign-valued inputs and outputs, and
suppose it computes the majority function on three signs, with ties assigned the
positive sign. There exist a coordinate $i\in\{0,1,2\}$ and a map
$j:\{−1,1\}\to\{0,1,2\}$ such that $j(a)\ne i$ for each sign $a$. For every input
$x\in\{−1,1\}^3$, the number of queries made by $T$ is at least $2$ if $x_i=x_{j(x_i)}$,
and at least $3$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Disagreement of a sign-dependent coordinate choice]
\lean{FABL.expect_majorityThree_skeleton_disagreement}
\label{FABL.expect_majorityThree_skeleton_disagreement}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.signCubeThreeEquiv}
\difficulty{4}
Let $x$ be uniformly distributed on the three-dimensional sign cube, let $i$ be one of
its three coordinates, and let $j$ assign to each sign one of the three coordinates,
always different from $i$. Then the probability that $x_i$ differs from the sign at
coordinate $j(x_i)$ is $1/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Hard input for three-bit majority]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeHardInput}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeHardInput}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube}
Given a sign $s$ and an index $i\in\{0,1,2\}$, let the three-coordinate input have value
$s$ at every coordinate except $i$, where its value is $-s$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Majority on a three-coordinate input]
\lean{FABL.majority_majorityThreeHardInput}
\label{FABL.majority_majorityThreeHardInput}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreeHardInput, FABL.signValue, FABL.thresholdSign}
\difficulty{4}
For every sign $s\in\{-1,1\}$ and every coordinate $j\in\{1,2,3\}$, form a
three-coordinate input whose $j$th entry is $-s$ and whose other two entries are $s$.
The majority function on this input equals $s$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Disagreement on a three-coordinate hard input]
\lean{FABL.expect_majorityThreeHardInput_skeleton_disagreement}
\label{FABL.expect_majorityThreeHardInput_skeleton_disagreement}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.majorityThreeHardInput}
\difficulty{4}
Choose $i\in\{0,1,2\}$ and a map $j:\{-1,1\}\to\{0,1,2\}$ such that $j(a)\ne i$
for both signs $a$. Choose a sign $s$ and an index $r\in\{0,1,2\}$ independently and
uniformly, and form the three-coordinate sign vector whose coordinate $r$ is $-s$ and
whose other coordinates are $s$. The probability that this vector differs from the
vector obtained by applying the same construction with sign equal to its $i$th
coordinate and index $j$ of that coordinate is $2/3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Randomized decision tree average cost]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCostUnder}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b003}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCostUnder}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.pmfExpectation}
Let $T$ be a randomized decision tree on $n$ coordinates with input alphabet $\Omega$
and output alphabet $\alpha$, and let $\mu$ be a probability distribution on the finite
input space $(\mathrm{Fin}\ n\to\Omega)$. Define the average cost of $T$ under $\mu$ as
the expectation, over inputs drawn from $\mu$, of its input cost.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Deterministic decision tree average query count]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.deterministicAverageCostUnder}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b003}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.deterministicAverageCostUnder}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.pmfExpectation}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let the input space $(\mathrm{Fin}\ n\to\Omega)$ be finite,
let $\mu$ be a probability distribution on that space, and let $T$ be a decision tree on
all $n$ coordinates with input alphabet $\Omega$ and output alphabet $\alpha$. Define
its average cost under $\mu$ to be the expected number of coordinates queried by $T$ on
an input drawn from $\mu$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Average cost as seed expectation]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCostUnder_eq_seedExpectation}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCostUnder_eq_seedExpectation}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCostUnder, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.deterministicAverageCostUnder, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.pmfExpectation}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $\Omega$ be a finite input alphabet, let
$\alpha$ be an output set, and let $f:\Omega^n\to\alpha$. For a finite randomized
decision tree $T$ computing $f$ and any probability distribution $\mu$ on the input
space, the average query cost of $T$ under $\mu$ equals the expectation, over the
random seed of $T$, of the deterministic tree's average query cost under $\mu$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Average cost bounded by worst-case cost]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCostUnder_le_worstCaseCost}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCostUnder_le_worstCaseCost}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCostUnder, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost_le_worstCaseCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_const, FABL.pmfExpectation_mono}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty input alphabet, let
$\alpha$ be an output set, and let $f:\Omega^n\to\alpha$. For any randomized
decision tree $T$ computing $f$ and any probability distribution $\mu$ on the input
space, the average query cost of $T$ under $\mu$ is at most its worst-case query cost
over all inputs.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Distribution of hard inputs]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeHardPMF}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeHardPMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.majorityThreeHardInput, FABL.uniformPMF}
Choose a sign uniformly from $\{-1,1\}$ and an index uniformly from $\{0,1,2\}$,
independently, and form the corresponding hard input. The resulting probability
distribution is the distribution of hard inputs on the three-coordinate sign cube.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Average query cost under the hard-input distribution]
\lean{FABL.deterministicAverageCostUnder_majorityThreeHardPMF}
\label{FABL.deterministicAverageCostUnder_majorityThreeHardPMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.deterministicAverageCostUnder, FABL.Sign, FABL.majorityThreeHardInput, FABL.majorityThreeHardPMF, FABL.pmfExpectation_map, FABL.pmfExpectation_uniformPMF_eq_expect}
\difficulty{3}
Let $T$ be a finite decision tree that queries three sign-valued coordinates and returns
a sign. Choose a seed uniformly from pairs $(s,r)$ with $s\in\{-1,1\}$ and
$r\in\{0,1,2\}$, and form the input whose $r$th coordinate is $-s$ and whose other two
coordinates are $s$. The average query cost of $T$ under the resulting input
distribution equals the expected number of queries made by $T$ on this seeded input.
\end{theorem}

Let $T$ be a finite decision tree on three sign-valued coordinates, with sign-valued
outputs, that computes majority on three signs (with ties assigned the positive sign).
Under the uniform distribution on the eight inputs, the expected number of queries made
by $T$ is at least $5/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Hard distribution lower bound for majority]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.majorityThree_hard_averageCost_ge}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.majorityThree_hard_averageCost_ge}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.exists_majorityThree_first_second, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.deterministicAverageCostUnder, FABL.Sign, FABL.deterministicAverageCostUnder_majorityThreeHardPMF, FABL.expect_majorityThreeHardInput_skeleton_disagreement, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreeHardInput, FABL.majorityThreeHardPMF}
\difficulty{4}
Let $T$ be a finite decision tree on three sign-valued coordinates, with sign-valued
outputs, that computes majority on three signs (with ties assigned the positive sign).
When the input is formed by choosing a sign and one of the three coordinates uniformly
and setting that coordinate to the opposite sign and the other two to the chosen sign,
the expected number of queries made by $T$ is at least $8/3$.
\end{theorem}

Every zero-error randomized decision tree computing majority on three signs has

\begin{definition}[Recursive ternary majority formula]
\lean{FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThree}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003}
\label{FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FormulaAddress, FABL.Sign, FABL.majority}
For each natural number $d$, define a function on sign assignments to the depth-$d$
address space by recursion: at depth $0$ it returns the assigned sign at the unique
address. At depth $d+1$, it applies three-input majority to the outputs of the depth-$d$
formulas in the three blocks indexed by $0,1,2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Address representation of recursive majority]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThree_eq_addressRecursiveMajorityThree}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThree_eq_addressRecursiveMajorityThree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.SignCube, FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThree, FABL.finFormulaAddressEquiv, FABL.recursiveMajority, FABL.recursiveMajority_succ}
\difficulty{4}
For every depth $d\in\mathbb{N}$ and every sign input $x$ indexed by the integers from
$0$ to $3^d-1$, recursive majority of depth $d$ on $x$ equals the address-based
recursive majority of depth $d$ on the function that assigns to each ternary formula
address the input sign at its corresponding index under the canonical indexing
equivalence.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Equivalence between signs and three blocks]
\lean{FABL.splitThreeBlocksEquiv}
\label{FABL.splitThreeBlocksEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign}
For any type $A$, a sign-valued function on $\{0,1,2\}\times A$ is equivalent to a
triple of sign-valued functions on $A$, obtained by restricting the first coordinate to
$0$, $1$, and $2$. The inverse assembles the three functions into one function on the
product.
\end{definition}

\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Factorization of a product average]
\lean{FABL.expect_triple_mul_separate}
\label{FABL.expect_triple_mul_separate}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.expect_pair_mul_separate}
\difficulty{3}
Let $A$, $B$, and $C$ be finite types, and let $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$, $g:B\to\mathbb{R}$,
and $h:C\to\mathbb{R}$. The uniform average of $f(a)g(b)h(c)$ over $(a,b,c)\in A\times
B\times C$ equals $(\mathbb{E}_a f(a))(\mathbb{E}_b g(b))(\mathbb{E}_c h(c))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Majority parity expectation identity]
\lean{FABL.expect_majorityThreeParity_step}
\label{FABL.expect_majorityThreeParity_step}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.expect_div_const, FABL.expect_triple_mul_separate}
\difficulty{4}
Let $A$ be a finite set and let $F,P:A\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $\mathbb E_{a\in
A}[P(a)]=0$, where expectation is uniform. For independent uniformly chosen $a,b,c\in
A$,
\[
\mathbb E\left[\frac{F(a)+F(b)+F(c)-F(a)F(b)F(c)}{2}\,P(a)P(b)P(c)\right]
=-\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbb E_{a\in A}[F(a)P(a)]\right)^3.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Top correlation of recursive majority]
\lean{FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThreeTopCoeff}
\label{FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThreeTopCoeff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThree, FABL.signValue, FABL.topCorrelation}
For each natural number $d$, the top correlation at depth $d$ is the top correlation of
the sign-valued address-recursive ternary-majority function at depth $d$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Top coefficient of recursive majority]
\lean{FABL.fourierCoeff_recursiveMajorityThree_univ_eq_addressTopCoeff}
\label{FABL.fourierCoeff_recursiveMajorityThree_univ_eq_addressTopCoeff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThree, FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThreeTopCoeff, FABL.finFormulaAddressEquiv, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.monomial, FABL.piReindexEquiv, FABL.recursiveMajority, FABL.recursiveMajorityThree_eq_addressRecursiveMajorityThree, FABL.signValue, FABL.topCorrelation, FABL.topCorrelation_reindex}
\difficulty{3}
For every nonnegative integer $d$, the Fourier coefficient on all coordinates of the
depth-$d$ recursive ternary majority function equals the top correlation of the
corresponding recursive majority formula on its leaf addresses.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Initial majority top coefficient]
\lean{FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThreeTopCoeff_zero}
\label{FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThreeTopCoeff_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThree, FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThreeTopCoeff, FABL.signValue, FABL.topCorrelation}
\difficulty{4}
The top coefficient of the depth-zero recursively composed three-input majority function
is $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Recurrence for the majority top coefficient]
\lean{FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThreeTopCoeff_succ}
\label{FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThreeTopCoeff_succ}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FormulaAddress, FABL.Sign, FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThree, FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThreeTopCoeff, FABL.expect_fullParity_eq_zero, FABL.expect_majorityThreeParity_step, FABL.majority, FABL.signValue, FABL.signValue_majority_three, FABL.splitThreeBlocksEquiv, FABL.topCorrelation}
\difficulty{4}
For every depth $d\in\mathbb{N}$, the top coefficient of the depth-$(d+1)$ recursively
composed three-input majority function equals minus one half the cube of the depth-$d$
top coefficient.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Nonvanishing of the majority top coefficient]
\lean{FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThreeTopCoeff_ne_zero}
\label{FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThreeTopCoeff_ne_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThreeTopCoeff, FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThreeTopCoeff_succ}
\difficulty{4}
For every depth $d\in\mathbb{N}$, the top correlation of the depth-$d$ recursively
composed three-input majority function is nonzero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Degree of recursive majority on three inputs]
\lean{FABL.fourierDegree_recursiveMajority_three}
\label{FABL.fourierDegree_recursiveMajority_three}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.addressRecursiveMajorityThreeTopCoeff_ne_zero, FABL.fourierCoeff_recursiveMajorityThree_univ_eq_addressTopCoeff, FABL.fourierDegree, FABL.fourierDegree_le_dimension, FABL.fourierDegree_le_iff, FABL.recursiveMajority}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $d$, the real-valued function obtained by converting the
recursively defined three-input majority function of depth $d$ to real values has
Fourier degree exactly $3^d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Recursive majority three depth le]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.recursiveMajorityThree_depth_le}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.recursiveMajorityThree_depth_le}
\leanok

\begin{definition}[Embedding of a recursive majority block]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockEmbedding}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockEmbedding}
\leanok
For each natural number $d$ and each block index $i\in\{0,1,2\}$, there is an injective
map from the $3^d$ coordinates into the $3^{d+1}$ coordinates that places each
coordinate in block $i$ under the canonical decomposition into three blocks of size
$3^d$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Coordinates in a recursive majority block]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockEmbedding}
For each natural number $d$ and each block index $i\in\{0,1,2\}$, the block coordinates
are the image of all $3^d$ coordinates under the embedding into block $i$ among the
$3^{d+1}$ coordinates.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Disjointness of three coordinate blocks]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates_disjoint}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates_disjoint}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates}
\difficulty{4}
Let $d\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $i,j\in\{0,1,2\}$ be distinct. The coordinate blocks in
the $(d+1)$st recursive three-way construction associated with $i$ and $j$ are disjoint.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Three block coordinates cover the full cube]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates_union}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates_union}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockEmbedding}
\difficulty{5}
For every natural number $d$, the three coordinate blocks obtained by fixing the first
coordinate to $0$, $1$, and $2$ partition the coordinates indexed by $\bbr^{3^{d+1}}$; in
particular, their union is all of $	ext{Fin}(3^{d+1})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Three-sign selector]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreePairValue}
\label{FABL.majorityThreePairValue}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign}
For signs $a,b,c\in\{\pm1\}$, define a sign-valued function by assigning $a$ if $a=b$,
and assigning $c$ if $a\ne b$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Pair rule agrees with three-sign majority]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreePairValue_eq_majority}
\label{FABL.majorityThreePairValue_eq_majority}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreePairValue, FABL.signValue, FABL.thresholdSign}
\difficulty{5}
For any three signs $a,b,c\in\{-1,1\}$, the rule that returns $a$ if $a=b$ and returns
$c$ otherwise agrees with majority of the three signs.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Three-Input Majority After a Swap]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreePairValue_swap_second_third}
\label{FABL.majorityThreePairValue_swap_second_third}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreePairValue, FABL.signValue, FABL.thresholdSign}
\difficulty{4}
For any three signs $a,b,c\in\{−1,1\}$, the value obtained by taking the majority of
$a,c,b$ is the majority of the three-input sign vector whose entries are $a,b,c$ in that
order.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Rotated Three-Input Majority]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreePairValue_rotate}
\label{FABL.majorityThreePairValue_rotate}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreePairValue, FABL.signValue, FABL.thresholdSign}
\difficulty{4}
For any three signs $a,b,c\in\{−1,1\}$, the value obtained by taking the majority of
$b,c,a$ is the majority of the three-input sign vector whose entries are $a,b,c$ in that
order.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Pair rule is invariant under reordering]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreePairValue_permutation}
\label{FABL.majorityThreePairValue_permutation}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreePairValue, FABL.signValue, FABL.thresholdSign}
\difficulty{5}
Let $i,j,k$ be pairwise distinct elements of $\{0,1,2\}$, and assign a sign
$v(r)\in\{-1,1\}$ to each index $r$. The rule that returns $v(i)$ if $v(i)=v(j)$ and
returns $v(k)$ otherwise equals the majority of the three assigned signs.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Majority continuation tree]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeContinuationTree}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b001}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeContinuationTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree, FABL.Sign}
Let $C$ be a finite set of available coordinates, let $a,b\in\{-1,1\}$, and let $T$ be a
decision tree using coordinates from $C$. Define a tree that is a leaf returning $a$
when $a=b$, and otherwise is $T$.
\end{definition}

  {FABL.queryCount_depthTwoInitialTree}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p044-b007,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p073-b004}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $C$ be a set of available coordinates among $n$
coordinates, and let $a,b\in\{−1,1\}$. For any decision tree $T$ using coordinates in
$C$ and any sign-valued input $x\in\{−1,1\}^{n}$, the continuation tree that stops when
$a=b$ and otherwise runs $T$ makes zero queries if $a=b$, and makes exactly as many
queries as $T$ does on $x$ if $a\ne b$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Ordered three-tree majority composition]
\lean{FABL.orderedMajorityThreeTree}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b001}
\label{FABL.orderedMajorityThreeTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.thenOnDisjoint, FABL.Sign, FABL.majorityThreeContinuationTree}
Let $A,B,C$ be finite sets of coordinates, with $A$ disjoint from $B\cup C$ and $B$
disjoint from $C$. Let $T_A,T_B,T_C$ be sign-valued decision trees using coordinates
from $A,B,C$, respectively. Define a tree that first runs $T_A$, then runs $T_B$, and
then uses the majority continuation rule with their two outputs and $T_C$; its available
coordinates are $A\cup(B\cup C)$.
\end{definition}

Let $n$ be a natural number, and let $A,B,C$ be pairwise disjoint sets of coordinates in
$	ext{Fin}(n)$, with $A$ disjoint from $B\cup C$ and $B$ disjoint from $C$. Given three
decision trees on these coordinate sets, with inputs and outputs in $\{ -1,1\}$, their
ordered composition evaluates on every input to the majority of the three tree outputs
(the common value of the first two when they agree, and otherwise the third).
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Decision tree embedded in a block]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeTreeInBlock}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeTreeInBlock}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.reindex, FABL.Sign, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockEmbedding}
For a natural number $d$, a block index $i\in\{0,1,2\}$, and a decision tree on the
$3^d$ coordinates with sign inputs and sign outputs, define the corresponding tree on
$3^{d+1}$ coordinates by relabelling each queried coordinate through the embedding into
block $i$. Its available coordinates are exactly the image of the $3^d$ coordinates in
that block.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Evaluation of a decision tree on one block]
\lean{FABL.eval_recursiveMajorityThreeTreeInBlock}
\label{FABL.eval_recursiveMajorityThreeTreeInBlock}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval_reindex, FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.recursiveInputBlock, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeTreeInBlock}
\difficulty{3}
Let $d$ be a nonnegative integer, let $i\in\{0,1,2\}$, and let $T$ be a finite decision
tree whose coordinates and input symbols are indexed by $\{0,\ldots,3^d-1\}$ and whose
outputs are signs. For every sign vector $x$ indexed by $\{0,\ldots,3^{d+1}-1\}$,
evaluating the tree obtained by embedding its coordinates into block $i$ of $x$ gives
the same output as evaluating $T$ on the restriction of $x$ to that block.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Query count in a recursive majority block]
\lean{FABL.queryCount_recursiveMajorityThreeTreeInBlock}
\label{FABL.queryCount_recursiveMajorityThreeTreeInBlock}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace_reindex_length, FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.recursiveInputBlock, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeTreeInBlock}
\difficulty{3}
Let $d$ be a nonnegative integer, let $i\in\{0,1,2\}$, and let $T$ be a finite
decision tree on sign inputs with $3^d$ coordinates. Embed those coordinates as block
$i$ among the $3^{d+1}$ coordinates, and let $x$ be a sign assignment on the larger
cube. The number of queries made by the reindexed tree on $x$ equals the number made by
$T$ on the restriction of $x$ to block $i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Recursive three-way seed space]
\lean{FABL.RecursiveMajorityThreeSeed}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003}
\label{FABL.RecursiveMajorityThreeSeed}
\leanok
Define a sequence of finite seed spaces by taking the depth-zero space to be a
singleton. At depth $d+1$, a seed consists of one of three block indices and an ordered
triple of seeds from the depth-$d$ space.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Recursive three-block majority tree]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeTree}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.castAvailable, FABL.RecursiveMajorityThreeSeed, FABL.Sign, FABL.orderedMajorityThreeTree, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates_disjoint, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates_union, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeTreeInBlock, FABL.recursiveNandIdentityTree}
For each depth $d$ and each seed in the recursively defined seed space, construct a
decision tree on $3^d$ sign coordinates. At depth zero it queries the sole coordinate;
at each greater depth it places three recursively constructed trees in the three
disjoint blocks and combines them in an order selected by the seed's block index.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Correctness of every seeded tree]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeTree_computes}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeTree_computes}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval_castAvailable, FABL.RecursiveMajorityThreeSeed, FABL.eval_orderedMajorityThreeTree, FABL.eval_recursiveMajorityThreeTreeInBlock, FABL.majorityThreePairValue_eq_majority, FABL.majorityThreePairValue_rotate, FABL.majorityThreePairValue_swap_second_third, FABL.recursiveMajority, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeTree, FABL.recursiveMajority_succ}
\difficulty{5}
For every depth $d\in\mathbb{N}$ and every seed in the recursively defined seed space at
depth $d$, the deterministic decision tree selected by that seed computes recursive
majority on inputs of length $3^d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Recursive majority tree query count]
\lean{FABL.queryCount_recursiveMajorityThreeTree_succ}
\label{FABL.queryCount_recursiveMajorityThreeTree_succ}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount_castAvailable, FABL.RecursiveMajorityThreeSeed, FABL.SignCube, FABL.eval_recursiveMajorityThreeTreeInBlock, FABL.queryCount_orderedMajorityThreeTree, FABL.queryCount_recursiveMajorityThreeTreeInBlock, FABL.recursiveInputBlock, FABL.recursiveMajority, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeTree, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeTree_computes}
\difficulty{5}
Let $d$ be a nonnegative integer, let $o\in\{0,1,2\}$, choose three seeds for depth
$d$, and let $x$ be a sign assignment on $3^{d+1}$ coordinates. The query count of the
depth-$d+1$ recursive majority tree is given by the following rule: if $o=0$, it is the
query count of the first depth-$d$ tree on block $0$, plus that of the second on block
$1$, plus zero when the recursive majority values on blocks $0$ and $1$ agree and
otherwise the query count of the third tree on block $2$. If $o=1$, use blocks $0$ and
$2$ first and, only when their recursive majority values differ, add the query count of
the second seed's tree on block $1$. If $o=2$, use blocks $1$ and $2$ first and, only
when their recursive majority values differ, add the query count of the first seed's
tree on block $0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Recursive three-way seed law]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeSeedLaw}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeSeedLaw}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RecursiveMajorityThreeSeed, FABL.uniformPMF}
Define a random seed recursively as follows. At depth $0$ it is the unique element of a
singleton set; at depth $d+1$, choose uniformly one of three orders and then choose
three independent seeds, each with the depth-$d$ law, recording the order and the three
seeds.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Randomized recursive majority tree]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003
}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RecursiveMajorityThreeSeed, FABL.Sign, FABL.recursiveMajority, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeSeedLaw, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeTree, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeTree_computes}
For each depth $d$, there is a randomized decision tree on $3^d$ sign coordinates that
computes the depth-$d$ recursive majority function with zero error for every seed. Its
finite, nonempty seed space is the recursively defined three-way seed space, equipped
with the specified seed distribution, and each seed selects the corresponding
deterministic recursive tree.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Successive input cost recurrence]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_inputCost_succ}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_inputCost_succ}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.SignCube, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_add, FABL.pmfExpectation_bind, FABL.pmfExpectation_const, FABL.pmfExpectation_map, FABL.pmfExpectation_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.queryCount_recursiveMajorityThreeTree_succ, FABL.recursiveInputBlock, FABL.recursiveMajority, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeSeedLaw, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeTree}
\difficulty{6}
For every depth $d\in\mathbb{N}$ and every sign input $x$ of length $3^{d+1}$, let
$x_0,x_1,x_2$ be its three length-$3^d$ blocks, let $c_i$ be the randomized tree's
expected query cost on $x_i$, and let $y_i$ be the recursive majority value on $x_i$.
The expected query cost at depth $d+1$ equals \[\frac{(c_0+c_1+\mathbf{1}_{y_0\ne
y_1}c_2)+(c_0+c_2+\mathbf{1}_{y_0\ne y_2}c_1)+(c_1+c_2+\mathbf{1}_{y_1\ne
y_2}c_0)}{3},\] where each indicator contributes its accompanying cost when its
condition holds and contributes zero otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Base-depth input cost]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_inputCost_zero}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_inputCost_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.SignCube, FABL.pmfExpectation_pure, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeSeedLaw, FABL.recursiveNandIdentityTree}
\difficulty{3}
For every sign input of length $3^0=1$, the randomized decision tree at depth zero has
expected query cost $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Pointwise input cost bound]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_inputCost_le}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_inputCost_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost_nonneg, FABL.SignCube, FABL.recursiveInputBlock, FABL.recursiveMajority, FABL.recursiveMajorityRandomizedCostBound, FABL.recursiveMajorityRandomizedCostBound_succ, FABL.recursiveMajorityRandomizedCostBound_zero, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_inputCost_succ, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_inputCost_zero}
\difficulty{5}
For every natural number $d$ and every sign vector $x$ of length $3^d$, the expected
query cost of the randomized recursive three-way majority tree on input $x$ is at most
$(8/3)^d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Worst-case query cost bound]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_worstCaseCost_le}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_worstCaseCost_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost, FABL.recursiveMajorityRandomizedCostBound, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_inputCost_le}
\difficulty{3}
For every depth $d\in\mathbb{N}$, the worst-case expected query cost of the randomized
decision tree for recursive majority on $3^d$ signs is at most $(8/3)^d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Recursive majority complexity bound]
\lean{FABL.randomizedDecisionTreeComplexity_recursiveMajority_three_le}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003}
\label{FABL.randomizedDecisionTreeComplexity_recursiveMajority_three_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.complexity, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost_nonneg, FABL.Sign, FABL.recursiveMajority, FABL.recursiveMajorityRandomizedCostBound, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_worstCaseCost_le}
\difficulty{4}
For each integer $d\geq 0$, define a function on $3^d$ signs recursively: at depth zero
it returns the sole input, and at depth $d+1$ it takes the majority of the outputs
obtained by applying the depth-$d$ function to each of three consecutive blocks of $3^d$
inputs. The randomized decision-tree complexity of this function, measured by the
infimum of the worst-case expected number of queried coordinates among finite-seed,
zero-error randomized decision trees, is at most $(8/3)^d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Three-block cube equivalence]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlocksEquiv}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlocksEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.piReindexEquiv}
For each natural number $d$, there is a canonical equivalence between sign vectors of
length $3^{d+1}$ and triples of sign vectors, each of length $3^d$, obtained by
splitting the coordinates into three consecutive blocks and arranging them as a function
from a three-element set to the blocks.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Recursive block equivalence evaluation]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlocksEquiv_apply}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlocksEquiv_apply}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.SignCube, FABL.recursiveInputBlock, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlocksEquiv}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $d$, sign vector $x\in\{−1,1\}^{3^{d+1}}$, and
$i\in\text{Fin}(3)$, evaluating the block decomposition of $x$ at $i$ gives the vector
of coordinates of $x$ in the $i$th block of length $3^d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Mean of recursive majority]
\lean{FABL.expect_recursiveMajorityThree_toReal_eq_zero}
\label{FABL.expect_recursiveMajorityThree_toReal_eq_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.SignCube, FABL.recursiveMajority, FABL.recursiveMajority_odd, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{4}
For every $d\in\mathbb N$, the expected real sign value of recursive three-ary majority
on a uniformly distributed input from $\{−1,1\}^{3^d}$ is zero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Recursive majority disagreement]
\lean{FABL.expect_recursiveMajorityThree_disagreement}
\label{FABL.expect_recursiveMajorityThree_disagreement}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.SignCube, FABL.expect_div_const, FABL.expect_pair_mul_separate, FABL.expect_recursiveMajorityThree_toReal_eq_zero, FABL.recursiveMajority, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{4}
For every depth $d\in\mathbb N$, if $X$ and $Y$ are independent uniformly distributed
sign vectors in $\{−1,1\}^{3^d}$, then the probability that their recursive three-ary
majority values differ is $1/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Average cost as uniform input expectation]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_averageCost_eq_expect}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_averageCost_eq_expect}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.pmfExpectation_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.productProbabilityPMF_uniformSign, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $d$, the average query cost of the randomized recursive
three-way majority tree under the uniform distribution on sign vectors of length $3^d$
equals the expected input cost when the input is drawn uniformly from that sign cube.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expected recursive tree pair cost]
\lean{FABL.expect_recursiveMajorityThree_pairCost}
\label{FABL.expect_recursiveMajorityThree_pairCost}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.expect_pair_mul_separate, FABL.expect_recursiveMajorityThree_disagreement, FABL.expect_triple_mul_separate, FABL.recursiveMajority, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree}
\difficulty{5}
For every $d\in\mathbb N$ and every pairwise distinct $i,j,k\in\{0,1,2\}$, let $c(x)$ be
the expected number of queries made by the randomized decision tree for recursive
three-ary majority on input $x$, and let $M(x)$ be its value. For three independent
uniformly distributed sign vectors $X_0,X_1,X_2\in\{−1,1\}^{3^d}$, the expected value of
$c(X_i)+c(X_j)+\mathbf{1}_{\{M(X_i)\ne M(X_j)\}}c(X_k)$ equals $\frac52$ times the
expected value of $c(X)$ for one uniformly distributed sign vector $X\in\{−1,1\}^{3^d}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Successive-level average cost recurrence]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_averageCost_succ}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_averageCost_succ}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.expect_div_const, FABL.expect_recursiveMajorityThree_pairCost, FABL.recursiveMajority, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlocksEquiv, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlocksEquiv_apply, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_averageCost_eq_expect, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_inputCost_succ, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $d$, the average query cost of the randomized recursive
three-way majority tree at level $d+1$ is $5/2$ times its average query cost at level
$d$, with uniform sign inputs at each level.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Base-level average query cost]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_averageCost_zero}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_averageCost_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost, FABL.Sign, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_averageCost_eq_expect, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_inputCost_zero, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{3}
At level $0$, the randomized recursive three-way majority tree has average query cost
$1$ under the uniform distribution on sign inputs.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Average cost of the randomized recursive majority tree]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_averageCost}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_averageCost}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost, FABL.Sign, FABL.recursiveMajorityAverageCostBound, FABL.recursiveMajorityAverageCostBound_succ, FABL.recursiveMajorityAverageCostBound_zero, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_averageCost_succ, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeRandomizedTree_averageCost_zero, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $d$, the average query cost of the randomized decision tree for
recursive three-way majority on uniformly distributed sign inputs of length $3^d$ is
$(5/2)^d$.
\end{theorem}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b001}
For every natural number $d$, under the uniform distribution on the sign cube of
dimension $3^d$, the minimum average query cost of a zero-error randomized decision tree
computing the $d$-fold recursive majority of three is at most $(5/2)^d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[First cyclic index]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicFirst}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicFirst}
\leanok
For an index $s\in\{0,1,2\}$, the first cyclic index is $s$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Second cyclic index]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicSecond}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicSecond}
\leanok
For an index $s\in\{0,1,2\}$, the second cyclic index is $1$ if $s=0$, $2$ if $s=1$, and
$0$ if $s=2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Third cyclic index]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicThird}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicThird}
\leanok
For an index $s\in\{0,1,2\}$, the third cyclic index is $2$ if $s=0$, $0$ if $s=1$, and
$1$ if $s=2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Distinctness of cyclic indices]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicSecond_ne_first}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicSecond_ne_first}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicFirst, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicSecond}
\difficulty{4}
For each seed $s\in\{0,1,2\}$, the cyclic successor of $s$ (where $2$ is followed by
$0$) differs from $s$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Distinctness of Two Cyclic Indices]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicThird_ne_first}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicThird_ne_first}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicFirst, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicThird}
\difficulty{4}
For each seed $s\in\{0,1,2\}$, define the first index to be $s$ and the third index to
be $2$ if $s=0$, $0$ if $s=1$, and $1$ if $s=2$. The third index is different from the
first.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Distinctness of the cyclic indices]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicThird_ne_second}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicThird_ne_second}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicSecond, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicThird}
\difficulty{4}
For each seed $s \in \{0,1,2\}$, define the second index by $1,2,0$ when $s=0,1,2$,
respectively, and the third index by $2,0,1$, respectively. The second and third indices
are different.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Cyclic majority decision tree]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicTree}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b001}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.Sign, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicFirst, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicSecond, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicSecond_ne_first, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicThird, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicThird_ne_first, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicThird_ne_second, FABL.majorityThreePairTree}
For each seed in a three-element set, define a decision tree on three sign coordinates
by applying the pairwise majority tree to the first, second, and third indices in the
cyclic ordering determined by that seed.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Evaluation of the Cyclic Decision Tree]
\lean{FABL.eval_majorityThreeCyclicTree}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b001}
\label{FABL.eval_majorityThreeCyclicTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval, FABL.SignCube, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicFirst, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicSecond, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicThird, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicTree, FABL.majorityThreePairTree, FABL.majorityThreePairValue}
\difficulty{5}
Let the sign alphabet be $\{-1,1\}$, let $s\in\{0,1,2\}$, and let $x$ assign a sign to
each of the three indices. Write $(i,j,k)$ for the cyclic ordering beginning at $s$. The
cyclic decision tree evaluates to $x_i$ when $x_i=x_j$, and to $x_k$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p044-b007,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p073-b004}
For every seed in $\{0,1,2\}$, the decision tree that queries the three coordinates in
the cyclic order determined by that seed computes majority on three signs. It returns
the repeated sign when the first two queried signs agree, and otherwise returns the
third; this equals $+1$ when the sum of the three signs is nonnegative and $-1$
otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Cyclic completion decision tree]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicCompletionTree}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicCompletionTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree, FABL.Sign, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicFirst, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicSecond, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicThird}
Given an index $s\in\{0,1,2\}$ and a known sign $k$, define a decision tree that first
queries the second cyclic coordinate. If its sign equals $k$, the tree returns $k$;
otherwise it queries the third cyclic coordinate and returns the sign found there. The
first cyclic coordinate is excluded from the available coordinates.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Evaluation of the Cyclic Completion Tree]
\lean{FABL.eval_majorityThreeCyclicCompletionTree}
\label{FABL.eval_majorityThreeCyclicCompletionTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval, FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicCompletionTree, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicSecond, FABL.majorityThreeCyclicThird, FABL.majorityThreePairValue}
\difficulty{4}
Let the sign alphabet be $\{-1,1\}$, let $s\in\{0,1,2\}$, and let $a$ be a sign. Define
$b$ and $c$ as the next and following indices in cyclic order modulo $3$ starting from
$s$. For any sign vector $x$ on these three indices, evaluating the completion tree with
seed $s$ and known value $a$ gives $a$ if $a=x_b$, and gives $x_c$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Decision tree with a distinct-output finish]
\lean{FABL.depthTwoFinishDifferent}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b001}
\label{FABL.depthTwoFinishDifferent}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.castAvailable, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.mapOutput, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.thenOnDisjoint, FABL.Sign, FABL.majorityThreePairValue}
Let $n$ be a natural number, and let $R_1,R_2,B_3$ be sets of coordinates in
$	ext{Fin}(n)$ such that $R_1$ is disjoint from $R_2\cup B_3$ and $R_2$ is disjoint from
$B_3$. Let $C_1$ and $C_2$ assign, to each sign, decision trees using coordinates in
$R_1$ and $R_2$, respectively, and let $E_3$ be a decision tree using coordinates in
$B_3$. For fixed signs $x_1,x_2$, the resulting decision tree first runs $E_3$,
producing a sign $y_3$. If $y_3=x_1$, it runs $C_1(x_1)$; if that produces $y_1=y_3$, it
returns $y_3$, and otherwise it runs $C_2(x_2)$ and returns the three-sign majority
value of $y_1,y_2,y_3$. If $y_3\ne x_1$, it runs $C_2(x_2)$; if that produces $y_2=y_3$,
it returns $y_3$, and otherwise it runs $C_1(x_1)$ and returns the three-sign majority
value of $y_1,y_2,y_3$. The resulting tree uses coordinates in $R_1\cup(R_2\cup B_3)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Decision tree for three-sign majority]
\lean{FABL.depthTwoFinishEqual}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b001}
\label{FABL.depthTwoFinishEqual}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.castAvailable, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.mapOutput, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.thenOnDisjoint, FABL.Sign, FABL.majorityThreePairValue}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $R_1,R_2,B_3\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ satisfy
$R_1\cap(R_2\cup B_3)=\varnothing$ and $R_2\cap B_3=\varnothing$, and let a sign mean an
element of $\mathbb Z^\times$. Suppose $C_1$ and $C_2$ assign, to each sign, a decision
tree querying only coordinates in $R_1$ and $R_2$, respectively, and let $E_3$ be a
decision tree querying only coordinates in $B_3$. For any fixed sign $x_1$, the
construction gives a decision tree querying only coordinates in $R_1\cup(R_2\cup B_3)$:
after the first tree returns $y_1$, it runs the second tree (with input $x_1$) before
$E_3$ if $y_1=x_1$, and otherwise runs $E_3$ before the second tree; when the next
observed sign equals $y_1$, it returns $y_1$ immediately, and otherwise labels the
output by the three-sign majority value of the observed signs.
\end{definition}

\proofstep
  {FABL.queryCount_depthTwoInitialTree}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p073-b004}
Let $R_1,R_2,B_3$ be finite sets of coordinates in a finite coordinate space, with $R_1$
disjoint from $R_2\cup B_3$ and $R_2$ disjoint from $B_3$. Let $C_1$ and $C_2$ assign to
each sign a decision tree using coordinates in $R_1$ and $R_2$, respectively, and let
$E_3$ be a decision tree using coordinates in $B_3$. For a sign $x_1$ and any sign
assignment $x$ on the coordinate space, the tree formed by the equal-value completion
construction evaluates to the first two tree outputs if they agree, and otherwise to the
output of $E_3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Query count unchanged by relabelling outputs]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount_mapOutput}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount_mapOutput}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.mapOutput, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace_mapOutput}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\Omega$, $\alpha$, and $\beta$ be types, let
$A\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, and let $g:\alpha\to\beta$. For any finite decision tree
$T$ with available set $A$ and any input $x:\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\to\Omega$, replacing each
leaf label $a$ by $g(a)$ does not change the number of queries made on $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Query count for the disjoint completion procedure]
\lean{FABL.queryCount_depthTwoFinishEqual}
\label{FABL.queryCount_depthTwoFinishEqual}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount_castAvailable, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount_mapOutput, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount_thenOnDisjoint, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace, FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.depthTwoFinishEqual}
\difficulty{5}
Let $R_1,R_2,B_3$ be finite sets of coordinates in an $n$-coordinate cube, with $R_1$
disjoint from $R_2\cup B_3$ and $R_2$ disjoint from $B_3$. For each sign, let $C_1$ and
$C_2$ be decision trees querying coordinates from $R_1$ and $R_2$, respectively, and let
$E_3$ be a decision tree querying coordinates from $B_3$. Fix a sign $x_1$ and an input
$x\in\{\pm1\}^n$. The query count of the combined procedure is the query count of
$C_1(x_1)$ plus the following: if $C_1(x_1)$ evaluates to $x_1$, add the query count of
$C_2(x_1)$ and then add zero if $C_2(x_1)$ evaluates to the value of $C_1(x_1)$, or
otherwise add the query count of $E_3$; if $C_1(x_1)$ does not evaluate to $x_1$, add
the query count of $E_3$ and then add zero if $E_3$ evaluates to the value of
$C_1(x_1)$, or otherwise add the query count of $C_2(x_1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Initial coordinate in a depth-two block]
\lean{FABL.depthTwoInitialCoordinate}
\label{FABL.depthTwoInitialCoordinate}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicFirst, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockEmbedding}
For a block index $b\in\{0,1,2\}$ and a seed index $s\in\{0,1,2\}$, define the initial
coordinate to be the coordinate assigned to block $b$ and the first cyclic index of $s$
by the depth-one recursive three-block embedding.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Initial coordinate at depth two]
\lean{FABL.depthTwoInitialCoordinates}
\label{FABL.depthTwoInitialCoordinates}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.depthTwoInitialCoordinate}
For blocks $b$ and seeds $s$ in a three-element set, the initial-coordinate set at depth
two is the singleton containing the depth-two initial coordinate determined by $b$ and
$s$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Remaining coordinates at depth two]
\lean{FABL.depthTwoRemainingCoordinates}
\label{FABL.depthTwoRemainingCoordinates}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.majorityThreeCyclicFirst, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockEmbedding}
For blocks $b$ and seeds $s$ in a three-element set, the remaining-coordinate set at
depth two consists of the recursive embedding, at level one, of every element of a
three-element set other than the cyclic-majority first coordinate determined by $s$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Initial and remaining coordinates partition a block]
\lean{FABL.depthTwoInitial_union_remaining}
\label{FABL.depthTwoInitial_union_remaining}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.depthTwoInitialCoordinate, FABL.depthTwoInitialCoordinates, FABL.depthTwoRemainingCoordinates, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates}
\difficulty{3}
For any block index $b$ and seed index $s$ in $\{0,1,2\}$, the union of the singleton
containing coordinate $s$ in block $b$ and the other two coordinates of that block is
exactly the set of all three coordinates in block $b$ in the nine-coordinate array.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Disjoint initial and remaining coordinates]
\lean{FABL.depthTwoInitial_remaining_disjoint}
\label{FABL.depthTwoInitial_remaining_disjoint}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.depthTwoInitialCoordinates, FABL.depthTwoRemainingCoordinates, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockEmbedding}
\difficulty{4}
For any two indices $b,s\in\{0,1,2\}$, take the three coordinates of the $b$th block in
a nine-coordinate array, indexed by $j\in\{0,1,2\}$. The singleton consisting of the
coordinate indexed by $s$ is disjoint from the set of the other two coordinates in that
block.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Initial coordinate lies in its block]
\lean{FABL.depthTwoInitial_subset_block}
\label{FABL.depthTwoInitial_subset_block}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.depthTwoInitialCoordinates, FABL.depthTwoInitial_union_remaining, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates}
\difficulty{1}
For any block index $b$ and seed index $s$ in $\{0,1,2\}$, the coordinate indexed by $s$
in the $b$th block of a nine-coordinate array belongs to the set of all three
coordinates in that block.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Remaining coordinates lie in their block]
\lean{FABL.depthTwoRemaining_subset_block}
\label{FABL.depthTwoRemaining_subset_block}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.depthTwoInitial_union_remaining, FABL.depthTwoRemainingCoordinates, FABL.recursiveMajorityThreeBlockCoordinates}
\difficulty{1}
For any block and seed in $\{0,1,2\}$, the coordinates in that block other than the one
selected first by the seed are contained in the block's full set of coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Initial depth-two query tree]
\lean{FABL.depthTwoInitialTree}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b001}
\label{FABL.depthTwoInitialTree}
\leanok

\begin{definition}[Depth-two block completion tree]

tree on nine sign coordinates by placing the cyclic-majority completion tree for that

nine sign coordinates by transporting the cyclic three-input majority tree with seed $s$

in that block under the canonical block embedding.

\begin{definition}[Completion model cost]

recursive input map for block $b$ to $x$, then evaluate it at the first and second
cyclic positions selected by $s$. The cost is $2$ if these two signs agree and $3$
otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Ordered interleaved model cost]
\lean{FABL.depthTwoInterleavedModelCostOrdered}

\uses{FABL.SignCube, FABL.depthTwoBlockModelValue, FABL.depthTwoCompletionModelCost, FABL.depthTwoEvaluationModelCost, FABL.depthTwoInitialCoordinate}
Let $x$ assign a sign to each of nine coordinates. Choose three block indices
$b_1,b_2,b_3\in\{0,1,2\}$ and three seed indices $s_1,s_2,s_3\in\{0,1,2\}$. Write $x_i$

$C_i$ for the completion cost at $(b_i,s_i)$, and $E_3$ for the evaluation cost at
$(b_3,s_3)$. The cost is $2$ plus the following quantity: if $x_1=x_2$, it is $C_1+C_2$
when $y_1=x_1$ and $y_2=y_1$, is $C_1+E_3$ when $y_1=x_1$ and $y_2\ne y_1$, is $C_1+E_3$
when $y_1\ne x_1$ and $y_3=y_1$, and is $E_3+C_2$ otherwise; if $x_1\ne x_2$, it is
$E_3+C_1$ when $y_3=x_1$ and $y_1=y_3$, is $E_3+C_2$ when $y_3=x_1$ and $y_1\ne y_3$, is
$C_2$ when $y_3\ne x_1$ and $y_2=y_3$, and is $C_2+C_1$ otherwise.
